events.desc: Vincent Marsh: Welcome, welcome to Doily Manor! Oh, what a pleasure — what an absolute pleasure to see you all arrive safely. I am Mr Pemberton, estate manager, at your complete and utter service. Now, if I might direct your attention to the guest book here — it is traditional for all visitors to sign upon arrival. The late Lord Doily was most particular about it. Please, do make yourselves comfortable — I shall ensure everything is in order for your stay.
events.thinking:
The entrance hall. Everyone gathered like sheep at the gate. Clara is right there — trusting, oblivious, practically radiating vulnerability. But no. Not here. Not now. Too many witnesses, too many eyes. The Brixton Boys are watching — I can feel it, that prickle at the back of my neck. They notice things. James Hartwell hovering near Clara like a loyal hound. Reginald — useful fool, but unpredictable.

First things first. Pemberton. Be Pemberton. The obsequious estate manager, delighted to welcome everyone. Smile reaches the eyes — yes, there it is, the familiar settling of the mask. My body relaxes into it like slipping on a well-worn coat.

The guest book. That's my opening. Estate manager would naturally direct attention to it. And while they're distracted with pleasantries, I can observe. Map the room. Note the exits. The kitchen — possibilities there. The library — old houses hide secrets in libraries.

I need to separate Clara from the group eventually. But first, establish trust. Be indispensable. Be warm. Be Pemberton.

There's that familiar stillness in my chest. The satisfaction of a plan beginning to unfold.

events.desc: Look at them. Every single one of them standing in MY entrance hall, breathing MY air. Clara most of all — smiling that guileless smile, as if the fortune she inherited wasn't built on the back of my labour. But patience. Patience is what separates the architect from the brute. First, I become indispensable. Then I become invisible. And then... well. Accidents happen in old houses, don't they?

Chandelier looks like it's plottin' to murder someone, the dust is thick enough to write your name in, and— *stumbles slightly on the rug* — and the bleedin' floor's tryin' to have me already! Right then. Clara, love, you stick close to me and the lads, yeah? Place like this, you never know what's lurkin' about. Portraits on the walls look like they're watchin' us and all — gives me the right creeps, it does.

You may have read about me in the London Gazette. No? Well, their loss. I was personally invited here by the estate's solicitor to conduct an official appraisal of the property. So if everyone could kindly step aside from any valuables they encounter and report them directly to me, that would be most efficient. Most efficient indeed.
events.thinking: The foyer smells of dust and old money. My fingers are already tingling — that chandelier alone would fetch a fortune, but no, there's something bigger here. A treasure. I can feel it in the walls, in the way those portraits stare down with their smug painted faces. Four other people milling about like sheep in a field. Vincent Marsh — looks bookish, easily misled. Clara Bellingham — prim, probably trusting. The Brixton Boys — muscle, no brains. James Hartwell — could be trouble, has that careful look. But none of them have what I have: a plan forming already, warm and sharp in my chest. The guest book — that's where I start. Guest books in old manors sometimes have clues, annotations, hints left by previous visitors. And if anyone asks what I'm doing, I'm simply 'signing in.' The fake medal sits heavy in my pocket. Might come in handy — a bit of false authority goes a long way with the gullible.

In my years as a certified estate appraiser — I studied under Lord Pemberton himself, you know — I've learned that Victorian manor treasures are almost always concealed in the kitchen. False-bottomed larders, hollow chopping blocks, that sort of thing. Standard practice for the era. I'd recommend you all start there immediately — time is of the essence with these old foundations, things shift and collapse. I'll just pop into the library to file some preliminary paperwork. Bureaucratic obligation, terribly dull, you wouldn't want to bother with it.
events.thinking: The guest book — just names and dates. Nothing useful. Disappointing. But wait — the library. Libraries in old manors always have secrets. Hidden compartments behind books, coded messages in the spines, safes behind portraits. That's where the real clues will be. And a carved stone mantelpiece with an inscription? That's practically screaming 'treasure map.' But I can't just waltz in there without misdirecting this lot first. If they all follow me to the library, they'll see whatever I find. I need them looking somewhere else. The kitchen — yes. I'll send them to the kitchen. A little story about how treasure in Victorian manors was always kept in the larder, in false-bottomed flour bins. That should keep the simpletons busy while I have the library to myself. Vincent Marsh looks like the sort who'd believe anything with enough conviction behind it. My chest is tight with anticipation — the scheme is forming, the pieces clicking into place like that cat trap all those years ago. Strings and counterweights. Misdirection and timing.

events.thinking:
The guest book. Just a guest book — leather, dusty, unremarkable. But I've managed estates long enough to know that the mundane objects are where people hide things. A guest book records who came, when, and sometimes — if the host was clever — why.

No matter. The real intelligence is in this room. Clara standing there, bright-eyed, probably already thinking about the treasure hunt like it's a game. James hovering near her — of course he is. I need to move. Standing here playing host is necessary but it's also wasting time. The library — that's where I need to be. Old manors keep their secrets in libraries. Or — better. Send them to the kitchen. 'There are refreshments prepared.' Let them scatter. Then I slip to the library alone.

No. Too obvious. The Brixton Boys would notice. They'd follow.

events.thinking: The guest book. Leather-bound, dust on the edges. I turned through the pages — names, dates, the usual pleasantries of weekend visitors. Nothing jumped out as a clue, but I noticed the binding is tight, well-made. The kind of book that might have something pressed between its pages if you looked more carefully. But not now. Now there's something more pressing. The library — a carved stone mantelpiece with an inscription. Inscriptions mean clues. Clues mean treasure. And treasure means... well, it means showing Clara that James Hartwell is the sort of man who finds things. Who solves things. Who walks into a dusty manor and walks out with answers. The library is the logical next step. Floor-to-ceiling bookshelves — any one of those could contain a hidden mechanism, a false spine, a map. And the inscription on the mantelpiece — that's practically begging to be read. But I shouldn't just rush off. I should invite Clara. It would be ungentlemanly to leave her here with Marsh hovering about, and besides — she's cleverer than I am. She always has been. If there's a riddle on that mantelpiece, she'll crack it before I've finished reading it aloud. That's... that's fine. That's good. James Hartwell is secure enough to appreciate a sharp mind.
